triggers: how do I check if a service is running
how do I see the status of a service
how to check a service
how do I know if something is running
what's the command to check a service
how do I check on the web server
answer:
InterGenOS uses **systemd**, so you manage services with `systemctl`:

```
systemctl status <name>      # is it running? recent log lines
systemctl is-active <name>   # just active / inactive
systemctl is-enabled <name>  # will it start at boot?
```

For example `systemctl status sshd`. Reading status needs no privileges; the service name is usually the daemon's name (sshd, NetworkManager, cups).

triggers: how do I start a service
how do I stop a service
how do I restart a service
how to restart a daemon
what's the command to restart something
how do I bring a service back up
answer:
Start, stop, or restart a service with `systemctl` (system services need `sudo`):

```
sudo systemctl start <name>
sudo systemctl stop <name>
sudo systemctl restart <name>     # stop then start
sudo systemctl reload <name>      # re-read config without dropping connections
```

For example `sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager`. Use `restart` after changing a service's configuration; `reload` if the service supports it and you don't want to interrupt it.

triggers: how do I make a service start at boot
how do I enable a service
how do I disable a service
how to stop a service starting automatically
how do I start something on boot
what's the command to enable a service
answer:
Whether a service starts automatically at boot is controlled by `enable` / `disable` (separate from whether it's running right now):

```
sudo systemctl enable <name>          # start at every boot
sudo systemctl enable --now <name>    # enable AND start it now
sudo systemctl disable <name>         # don't start at boot
```

`enable` only affects future boots — add `--now` to also start it immediately, or run `systemctl start` separately.

triggers: how do I see what services failed
how do I find failed services
how do I check service logs
how to see why a service crashed
how do I read the logs for a service
what's wrong with my services
answer:
List anything that failed, then read its log:

```
systemctl --failed                 # every unit in a failed state
journalctl -u <name> -b             # this boot's log for one service
journalctl -u <name> -e             # jump to the newest entries
```

Start with `systemctl --failed` to see what's broken, then `journalctl -u <name> -b` to find out why. `journalctl -xe` shows the most recent system-wide errors with explanations.

triggers: how does systemd work
what is systemd
explain systemd
how do services work on InterGenOS
tell me about systemd
how does the service manager work
answer:
**systemd** is InterGenOS's init system and service manager — it starts the system at boot and supervises long-running services (called *units*). You drive it with `systemctl`, and read its logs with `journalctl`:

```
systemctl status <name>      # is a service running? recent log
systemctl start|stop|restart <name>
systemctl enable|disable <name>    # start at boot, or not
systemctl --failed                 # anything that crashed
journalctl -u <name> -b             # this boot's log for a unit
```

A unit is usually named after its daemon (`sshd`, `NetworkManager`, `cups`). Reading status and logs needs no privileges; starting, stopping, and enabling do. systemd also handles timers, sockets, and mounts as units, but services are what you'll touch most.

triggers: how do I kill a frozen program
answer:
Find it and stop it:
```
pkill <name>                 # by name, e.g. pkill firefox
# still stuck? force it:
pkill -9 <name>
```
On the GNOME (Wayland) desktop you can also open **System Monitor**, select the app, and hit
**End Process**. Use `-9` (SIGKILL) only when a normal `pkill` doesn't work.

triggers: an app is not responding how do I close it
answer:
Try to close its window first; if that hangs, kill it by name:
```
pkill <name>          # graceful
pkill -9 <name>       # force, if it won't die
```
Or use GNOME **System Monitor** → select the app → **End Process**. On Wayland the old
`xkill` click-to-kill isn't available; use the name-based commands or System Monitor.

triggers: how do I force quit on linux
answer:
```
pkill -9 <name>       # force-kill every process matching that name
# or by PID:
kill -9 <pid>         # get the PID from `pgrep <name>` or System Monitor
```
`-9` is SIGKILL — the unconditional force-quit. Try a plain `pkill <name>` first so the app can
clean up. GNOME **System Monitor → End Process** is the graphical equivalent.

triggers: how do I kill a process by name
answer:
```
pgrep -a <name>       # list matching processes (verify before killing)
pkill <name>          # terminate them
pkill -9 <name>       # force, if needed
```

triggers: how do I make a program start automatically when I log in
answer:
This is a per-user desktop autostart (GNOME on Wayland). Drop a `.desktop` launcher in your
autostart folder:
```
mkdir -p ~/.config/autostart
cp /usr/share/applications/<app>.desktop ~/.config/autostart/
```
It will launch on your next login. (For a background *system* service, use
`sudo systemctl enable <service>` instead.) GNOME's **Settings** has no autostart pane by
default; the `~/.config/autostart` file is the reliable way.
